questions.q: By definition, tachyarrhythmias require a heart rate exceeding which threshold, and are morphologically classified into which two QRS complex durations?
opts: > 100 bpm; Narrow and Wide
> 90 bpm; Regular and Irregular
> 120 bpm; Monomorphic and Polymorphic
> 100 bpm; Normal and Peaked
questions.exp: Tachyarrhythmias are defined by HR > 100 bpm and are divided morphologically into narrow and wide QRS complexes. (Book p394)

questions.q: Which triad of fundamental electrophysiological mechanisms accounts for all tachyarrhythmias listed on this page?
opts: Enhanced automaticity, triggered activity, and re-entry
Decreased threshold, delayed repolarisation, and conduction block
Early repolarisation, ion channel arrest, and sodium overload
Parasystole, accelerated conduction, and wandering pacemaker
questions.exp: The three fundamental causes listed are enhanced automaticity, triggered activity, and re-entry. (Book p394)

questions.q: Ventricular impulses originating above the bifurcation of the Bundle of His traverse Purkinje fibers to produce bilateral synchronous activation and a normal/narrow QRS complex lasting ____.
questions.exp: Impulses originating above the His bifurcation conduct via Purkinje fibers yielding bilateral synchronous activation and a narrow QRS (< 0.12 s). (Book p394)

questions.q: When impulses arise below the bifurcation of the Bundle of His, how are the ventricles activated and what is the resulting QRS complex duration?
opts: Ventricular myocardium activates ventricles; Wide QRS (≥ 0.16 s)
Purkinje fibers activate ventricles; Narrow QRS (< 0.12 s)
Accessory bypass tract conducts impulse; Intermediate QRS (0.10 - 0.12 s)
Bundle branches conduct synchronously; Slightly wide QRS (0.12 - 0.14 s)
questions.exp: Below the His bifurcation, ventricular myocardium activates the ventricles directly, creating a wide QRS complex (≥ 0.16 s). (Book p394)

questions.q: An ECG reveals an SVT conducted with an underlying bundle branch block. According to the origin-of-impulses section, what is the expected QRS complex duration?
questions.exp: Supraventricular tachycardias associated with bundle branch block manifest with an intermediate QRS duration of 0.12 - 0.16 s. (Book p394)

questions.q: Match each tachyarrhythmia category to its characteristic QRS complex morphology — 1) Supraventricular tachycardia (SVT) 2) SVT with conduction block (RBBB/LBBB) 3) Ventricular tachycardia (VT) … A) Narrow QRS complex B) Slightly wide QRS C) Wide QRS
questions.exp: Under Classification: SVT yields narrow QRS; SVT with conduction block yields slightly wide QRS; VT yields wide QRS. (Book p394)

questions.q: Which statement regarding normal enhanced automaticity is accurate according to the mechanism diagram?
opts: True — Sinus tachycardia represents normal enhanced automaticity originating from normal sinus impulses at the SA node
True — Sinus tachycardia originates from ectopic atrial foci outside the SA node
False — Normal enhanced automaticity produces wide QRS complexes exceeding 0.16 s
False — Sinus tachycardia is driven exclusively by micro re-entry within the sinoatrial junction
questions.exp: Normal enhanced automaticity corresponds to sinus tachycardia, where normal sinus impulses originate from the SA node. (Book p394)

questions.q: Which finding is NOT correctly listed under abnormal enhanced automaticity on this page?
opts: Atrial tachycardia is driven solely by enhanced automaticity and cannot exhibit re-entry
Atrial tachycardia can be focal or multifocal and has all 3 mechanisms of tachycardia
Junctional tachycardia is listed under abnormal enhanced automaticity
Ventricular tachycardia (specifically ischemic VT) is listed under abnormal enhanced automaticity
questions.exp: The source specifically notes that atrial tachycardia (focal/multifocal) possesses all 3 mechanisms of tachycardia, not merely automaticity. (Book p395)

questions.q: A heart failure patient receiving digoxin presents with paroxysmal atrial tachycardia with AV block. Which metabolic disturbance precipitates this condition and what is the underlying mechanism?
opts: Hypokalemia; Tachycardia due to enhanced automaticity
Hyperkalemia; Tachycardia due to macro re-entry
Hypercalcemia; Tachycardia due to early afterdepolarisations
Hyponatremia; Tachycardia due to conduction block alone
questions.exp: PAT with AV block is associated with digoxin toxicity, precipitated by hypokalemia, and occurs due to enhanced automaticity. (Book p395)

questions.q: Under triggered activity, early afterdepolarisation (EAD) is linked to which clinical entity?
opts: Long QT syndrome leading to Torsades de pointes
Right ventricular outflow tract VT
Atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction
Brugada syndrome with pseudo-RBBB
questions.exp: Early afterdepolarisation is specifically paired with Long QT Syndrome and Torsades de pointes. (Book p395)

questions.q: A young athlete develops non-sustained VT during strenuous exertion. Electrophysiological testing demonstrates late afterdepolarisations driven by sympathetic tone and elevated intracellular calcium. Which rhythm fits this late afterdepolarisation category?
opts: Right ventricular outflow tract VT (RVOT VT)
Torsades de pointes in Long QT type 1
Atrioventricular nodal re-entrant tachycardia (AVNRT)
Scar-related post-infarction VT
questions.exp: Late afterdepolarisations cause catecholamine-sensitive arrhythmias (d/t sympathetic activity & elevated intracellular Ca2+), including RVOT VT, LVOT VT, and sympathetic VT. (Book p395)

questions.q: Re-entry tachycardias are classically precipitated by premature complexes (PAC/PVC) and are characteristically highly responsive to ____.
opts: DC cardioversion
Vagal maneuvers only
Intravenous magnesium sulfate
High-dose atropine infusion
questions.exp: Re-entry is precipitated by premature complexes (PAC/PVC) and is highly responsive to DC cardioversion. (Book p395)

questions.q: Match each arrhythmia to its re-entry circuit classification — 1) AVNRT 2) AVRT 3) Atrial fibrillation … A) Micro re-entry circuit in the AV node B) Macro re-entry circuit involving bypass tract C) Micro re-entry circuits in atrial tissue
questions.exp: Micro re-entry: AVNRT, Brugada syndrome, Atrial Fibrillation. Macro re-entry: AVRT, Atrial Flutter, Scar VT. (Book p395)

questions.q: Which statement accurately reflects the structural heart requirements for wide QRS ventricular tachycardia on this page?
opts: True — VT occurs only in a structurally abnormal heart (due to previous infarction or scar)
True — VT occurs primarily in completely normal hearts without pre-existing structural disease
False — Wide QRS tachycardias never arise from previous myocardial scars
False — Re-entrant narrow QRS tachycardias require prior extensive myocardial infarction
questions.exp: Under causes based on QRS, wide QRS VT (Scar VT/Long QT) is annotated: 'VT: Occurs only in a structurally abnormal heart (D/t previous infarction)'. (Book p395)

questions.q: When interpreting a narrow QRS tachycardia with 10 small boxes between consecutive R waves, what heart rate is calculated using the 1500 small-box rule?
opts: 150 bpm
120 bpm
180 bpm
200 bpm
questions.exp: HR calculation shown: HR = 1500 / 10 = 150 bpm, confirming tachycardia. (Book p396)

questions.q: Which sequence correctly reflects the frequency hierarchy of supraventricular tachycardias (m/c SVT) stated on this page?
opts: Sinus tachycardia > AF > AVNRT > AVRT > SART
AF > Sinus tachycardia > AVRT > AVNRT > SART
AVNRT > AVRT > AF > Sinus tachycardia > SART
Sinus tachycardia > AVNRT > AF > SART > AVRT
questions.exp: The printed hierarchy is: m/c SVT: Sinus tachycardia > AF > AVNRT > AVRT > SART. (Book p396)

questions.q: What are the baseline clinical features of AVNRT regarding cardiac structure, sex predilection, and clinical prognosis?
opts: Can occur in structurally normal heart; F > M; Good prognosis
Requires severe structural heart disease; M > F; Guarded prognosis
Occurs only after extensive MI; Equal sex ratio; Poor prognosis
Always associated with congenital ASD; F > M; High mortality
questions.exp: Features listed: Can occur in structurally normal heart; F > M; Good prognosis. (Book p396)

questions.q: In the dual AV nodal pathway model, the slow pathway conducts slowly and has a ____ refractory period, whereas the fast pathway conducts rapidly and has a longer refractory period.
opts: shorter
longer
variable
permanent
questions.exp: Slow pathway: conducts slowly, shorter refractory period. Fast pathway: conducts rapidly, longer refractory period. (Book p396)

questions.q: A premature supraventricular beat arrives when the fast AV nodal pathway is refractory but the slow pathway has recovered. How does the impulse circulate to sustain AVNRT?
opts: Impulse enters slow pathway, activates ventricles, and joins fast pathway retrogradely to activate atria
Impulse enters fast pathway, activates atria antegradely, and exits via the accessory bypass tract
Impulse blocks antegradely in both pathways and travels down the His bundle via ventricular myocardium
Impulse circulates entirely within the left atrium without engaging the AV junction
questions.exp: The premature impulse enters the recovered slow pathway, splits to reach ventricles (narrow QRS), and joins the fast pathway retrogradely to activate atria. (Book p396)

questions.q: Due to retrograde activation of the atria via the fast pathway during AVNRT, what P-wave morphology is characteristically seen in the inferior leads (II, III, and aVF)?
opts: P waves are inverted in leads II, III and aVF
P waves are peaked and upright > 2.5 mm in II, III and aVF
P waves are bifid with a terminal negative deflection in lead II
P waves are completely flat and isoelectric across all leads
questions.exp: Retrograde activation of atria results in P waves that are inverted in leads II, III and aVF. (Book p396)

questions.q: In what proportion of AVNRT patients are the P and QRS complexes formed simultaneously, causing the P wave to be completely buried within the QRS complex?
opts: 2/3rd of patients
1/3rd of patients
1/10th of patients
95% of patients
questions.exp: The text states: '2/3rd patients: P & QRS formed simultaneously -> P wave buried in QRS complex.' (Book p397)

questions.q: A regular narrow-complex tachycardia runs at a rate of 210 bpm. What physiological boundary excludes sinus tachycardia and which diagnosis is strongly favored?
opts: Sinus cannot maintain rate > 180 bpm; Rate 200–250 bpm favors AVNRT >> AVRT
Sinus cannot maintain rate > 150 bpm; Rate > 200 bpm favors atrial flutter exclusively
Sinus cannot maintain rate > 220 bpm; Rate 200–250 bpm favors ventricular tachycardia
Sinus cannot maintain rate > 100 bpm; Rate > 200 bpm favors junctional tachycardia
questions.exp: Sinus cannot maintain rate > 180 bpm; at a rate of 200 - 250 bpm, AVNRT >> AVRT. (Book p397)

questions.q: Match each feature of atypical AVNRT to its clinical detail — 1) Incidence of atypical AVNRT 2) Triggering premature beat 3) Differential diagnosis on ECG … A) 5% of cases B) Premature ventricular complex (PVC) C) Atrial tachycardia
questions.exp: Table shows: Typical (95%, PAC, Slow-Fast) vs Atypical (5%, PVC trigger, Fast-Slow pathway, D/d Atrial tachycardia). (Book p397)

questions.q: While typical AVNRT enters via the slow pathway and exits via the fast pathway, atypical AVNRT conducts antegradely by entering the ____ pathway and exiting via the slow pathway.
opts: Fast
Accessory
Mahaim
Kent
questions.exp: Under Pathway in the table: Typical enters Slow; exit Fast. Atypical enters Fast; exit Slow. (Book p397)

questions.q: In the 1/3rd of typical AVNRT patients where P waves fall outside the QRS complex, which pseudo-wave description is NOT listed?
opts: Pseudo delta wave: P wave distorting the initial PR segment
Pseudo S wave: P wave just outside QRS
Pseudo r' wave: P wave on r wave
Pseudo Q wave: P wave just before Q wave
questions.exp: The three listed pseudo waves on p398 are Pseudo S wave, Pseudo r' wave, and Pseudo Q wave. Pseudo delta wave is not part of this list. (Book p398)

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman in regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 205 bpm receives a rapid IV push of adenosine. Which electrocardiographic response is demonstrated on the rhythm strip?
opts: Conversion of AVNRT back to normal sinus rhythm
Immediate acceleration into ventricular fibrillation
Persistent tachycardia with progressive PR prolongation
Development of complete third-degree heart block requiring pacing
questions.exp: The strip caption states: 'Can be converted to normal rhythm by adenosine', showing abrupt termination into normal sinus rhythm. (Book p398)

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the clinical associations and relative frequency of AVRT compared to AVNRT?
opts: True — AVRT is rarer than AVNRT and is fundamentally associated with WPW syndrome
True — AVRT is far more common than AVNRT and occurs exclusively in elderly patients
False — AVRT has no association with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome or bypass tracts
False — AVNRT is an extranodal macro re-entry tachycardia whereas AVRT is strictly intranodal
questions.exp: Under AVRT: Features: Rarer than AVNRT; Associated with WPW syndrome. (Book p398)

questions.q: Match each AVRT subtype to its impulse entry limb and resulting QRS complex width — 1) Orthodromic AVRT entry 2) Orthodromic AVRT QRS 3) Antidromic AVRT entry 4) Antidromic AVRT QRS … A) AV node B) Narrow QRS C) Bundle of Kent D) Wide QRS
questions.exp: Orthodromic AVRT: Entry AV node, Exit Bundle of Kent, Narrow QRS. Antidromic AVRT: Entry Bundle of Kent, Exit AV node, Wide QRS. (Book p398)

questions.q: In orthodromic AVRT initiated by a well-timed PAC, which anatomical sequence describes the path of impulse propagation?
opts: Enters AV node slowly, activates ventricles synchronously, conducts retrogradely via bypass tract, and re-enters AV node
Enters bypass tract rapidly, activates ventricles eccentrically, conducts retrogradely via AV node, and re-enters bypass tract
Blocks in AV node, travels down His bundle via slow pathway, and exits through ventricular myocardium
Enters pulmonary veins, activates left atrium, conducts retrogradely via sinus venosus, and terminates
questions.exp: Orthodromic AVRT: PAC enters AV node (conducted slowly), both ventricles activated synchronously, impulse enters bypass tract from ventricles to atrium retrogradely, and re-enters AV node. (Book p399)

questions.q: On the ECG of orthodromic AVRT, the retrograde P wave falls just outside the QRS complex with an RP interval measured as:
opts: 2 small boxes (~ 80 – 100 ms)
0.5 small box (~ 20 ms)
5 small boxes (~ 200 ms)
8 small boxes (~ 320 ms)
questions.exp: ECG findings for orthodromic AVRT state: RP interval: 2 boxes ~ 80 - 100 ms, where P falls just outside QRS. (Book p399)

questions.q: Comparing AVNRT versus AVRT in the summary table, which parameter is NOT correctly paired?
opts: Underlying structural disease: AVNRT is linked to WPW syndrome, whereas AVRT has no structural link
Synchronous A-V activation: Present (+) in AVNRT, absent (-) in AVRT
RP interval: < 80 ms in AVNRT, 80 – 100 ms in AVRT
Re-entry circuit: Micro re-entry in AVNRT, macro re-entry in AVRT
questions.exp: Structural heart disease is absent (-) in AVNRT and associated with WPW syndrome in AVRT. The option reverses this association. (Book p399)

questions.q: Both AVNRT and AVRT are categorized overall as short RP, long PR tachycardias; however, AVNRT displays an ultra-short RP interval of ____, while AVRT exhibits an RP interval of 80–100 ms.
opts: < 80 ms
< 20 ms
questions.exp: In the comparison table, the RP interval is < 80 ms in AVNRT and 80 - 100 ms in AVRT. (Book p399)

questions.q: Which statement regarding the hemodynamic status of patients with AVNRT compared to AVRT is stated in the comparison table?
opts: True — AVNRT patients are characteristically stable, whereas AVRT patients may be stable or unstable
True — AVNRT patients are uniformly hemodynamically unstable requiring immediate DC shocks
False — AVRT patients are never hemodynamically unstable regardless of heart rate
False — Both AVNRT and AVRT uniformly cause immediate cardiogenic shock
questions.exp: In the table under Hemodynamic status: AVNRT is 'Stable', whereas AVRT is 'Stable/unstable'. (Book p399)

questions.q: According to the concluding note on page 399, what distinct interval pattern differentiates atrial tachycardia from AVNRT and AVRT?
opts: Long RP, short PR
Short RP, long PR
Short RP, short PR
Long RP, long PR
questions.exp: The note explicitly highlights: 'Atrial tachycardia: Long RP, short PR.' (Book p399)

questions.q: Why is producing an AV nodal block the shared primary therapeutic goal in AVNRT, AVRT, and atrial tachycardia?
opts: Because all three tachyarrhythmias operate through the AV node
Because the AV node is the primary source of ectopic ventricular automaticity
Because AV nodal blockade eliminates sympathetic outflow to peripheral vessels
Because the AV node directly dissolves micro re-entry within the coronary sinus
questions.exp: Under Goal: AVNRT, AVRT, Atrial tachycardia operate through AV Node -> mx: AV nodal block. (Book p400)

questions.q: A patient in rapid narrow-complex tachycardia presents with severe hypotension (BP 70/40 mmHg) and acute pulmonary edema. What is the immediate treatment of choice?
opts: Synchronised DC cardioversion
Intravenous adenosine 6 mg rapid push
Intravenous verapamil 5 mg infusion over 2 minutes
Oral metoprolol 50 mg loading dose
questions.exp: For hemodynamically unstable patients, the indicated management is immediate synchronised DC cardioversion. (Book p400)

questions.q: In a hemodynamically stable patient with SVT, which agent is the drug of choice (DOC) for AV nodal block, and what is its dual mechanism of action?
opts: Adenosine; Blocks PAC in AVNRT/AVRT and decreases HR in atrial tachycardia
Verapamil; Prolongs ventricular refractoriness and terminates sinus node firing
Digoxin; Directly cardioverts macro re-entry and stimulates vagal tone
Amiodarone; Blocks fast sodium channels and inhibits thyroid release
questions.exp: DOC for AV nodal block in stable patients is Adenosine. MOA: AVNRT/AVRT: Blocks PAC; Atrial tachycardia: decreases HR. (Book p400)

questions.q: What are the elimination half-life, arm-to-arm transit time, and arm-to-heart circulation time of intravenous adenosine?
opts: T1/2: 6 s; Arm to arm: 15 s; Arm to heart: 7.5 s
T1/2: 30 s; Arm to arm: 60 s; Arm to heart: 20 s
T1/2: 2 min; Arm to arm: 10 s; Arm to heart: 5 s
T1/2: 6 s; Arm to arm: 30 s; Arm to heart: 15 s
questions.exp: Pharmacokinetics of adenosine: T1/2: 6 s; Arm to arm circulation: 15 s; Arm to heart circulation: 7.5 s. (Book p400)

questions.q: What is the initial recommended bolus dose of adenosine via the brachial vein, and what is the cumulative maximum dose when repeated?
opts: 6 mg initial bolus; repeat 12 mg + 12 mg up to max 30 mg
3 mg initial bolus; repeat 6 mg + 6 mg up to max 15 mg
12 mg initial bolus; repeat 12 mg up to max 24 mg
6 mg initial bolus; repeat 6 mg up to max 18 mg
questions.exp: Administration: 6 mg through brachial vein (Repeat: 12 mg + 12 mg, max: 30 mg), followed by immediate saline flush/push/chase. (Book p400)

questions.q: During the administration of adenosine via a peripheral line, what procedural posture and arm position are instructed on page 400 to optimize drug delivery?
opts: Put patient in 45° supine position, administer adenosine, then shift patient to prone position and raise arm overhead
Keep patient strictly upright at 90°, administer adenosine, and lower both arms below heart level
Position patient in steep Trendelenburg at -30° throughout administration with bilateral leg elevation
Place patient in left lateral decubitus with arm held flush against the chest wall
questions.exp: Procedure: Put patient in 45° supine position -> Administer adenosine -> Shift patient to prone position + Raise arm overhead. (Book p400)

questions.q: Why is it mandatory to have a defibrillator immediately ready when administering adenosine to a patient with suspected AVRT?
opts: Adenosine can trigger atrial fibrillation which degenerates via the bypass tract: AF -> VT -> VF -> Death
Adenosine routinely precipitates rupture of the interventricular septum during SVT
Adenosine induces prolonged electrical systole and permanent electromechanical dissociation
Adenosine causes severe hypocalcemia triggering immediate asystole
questions.exp: Safety protocol: Have defibrillator ready: If AVRT treated with adenosine -> AF -> VT -> VF -> Death. (Book p400)

questions.q: A known patient with COPD and bronchial asthma develops stable AVNRT. Why is adenosine contraindicated, and which alternative drug dosages are listed?
opts: Causes bronchospasm; alternatives are verapamil 2.5–5 mg IV (max 15 mg), metoprolol 5 mg IV (max 15 mg), or esmolol
Causes laryngospasm; alternatives are amiodarone 300 mg bolus or flecainide 100 mg orally
Causes metabolic acidosis; alternatives are atropine 1 mg IV or dopamine infusion
Causes coronary vasodilation; alternatives are digoxin 0.5 mg IV or sotalol 80 mg IV
questions.exp: Adenosine is contraindicated in COPD/BA as it can cause bronchospasm. Alternatives: verapamil 2.5-5 mg IV (max 15 mg), metoprolol 5 mg IV (max 15 mg), or esmolol. (Book p400)

questions.q: Which pharmacological agent is specifically indicated for managing AVNRT occurring in a patient with concurrent congestive heart failure?
opts: Digoxin
Verapamil
Metoprolol
Esmolol
questions.exp: Under alternatives/protocols on p400: 'Heart failure with AVNRT: Digoxin.' (Book p400)

questions.q: What are the clinical features and underlying heart status in atrial tachycardia?
opts: Structurally abnormal heart; chronic runs cause tachyarrhythmia-related cardiomyopathy; follows all 3 mechanisms (m/c enhanced automaticity)
Structurally normal heart; never causes cardiomyopathy; follows re-entry exclusively
Congenital accessory pathway; young athletic males; triggered early afterdepolarisations
Severe coronary calcification; elderly smokers; isolated macro re-entry circuits
questions.exp: Features: Structurally abnormal heart; Chronic: Tachyarrhythmia related cardiomyopathy; Follows all 3 mechanisms of tachycardia (m/c: enhanced automaticity). (Book p401)

questions.q: What is the primary management strategy for atrial tachycardia to restore sinus rhythm, and what is reserved for rare failures?
opts: Rate reduction using beta-blockers (metoprolol) or CCBs (verapamil); antiarrhythmics on failure
Immediate high-energy unsynchronized defibrillation followed by magnesium
Primary catheter ablation within 2 hours of symptom onset
Observation alone without pharmacological rate slowing
questions.exp: Management: decrease Rate -> Sinus rhythm with beta-blockers (metoprolol) or CCB (verapamil); failure (rare) -> Antiarrhythmics. (Book p401)

questions.q: An ECG demonstrates a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150 bpm with uniform abnormal P waves, long RP, and short PR intervals. Over several minutes, the rate slowly accelerates before gradually slowing down. What rhythm and phenomenon does this represent?
opts: Unifocal atrial tachycardia exhibiting warm-up and cool-down phenomenon
Typical AVNRT with sudden paroxysmal onset and termination
Orthodromic AVRT with variable accessory pathway conduction
Atrial flutter with fluctuating 3:1 and 4:1 AV block
questions.exp: Unifocal AT: Narrow QRS, Rate ~150 bpm, regular rhythm, uniform abnormal P waves, RP Long, PR Short. Note: Warm up & cool down phenomenon (slow increase & decrease of rate). (Book p401)

questions.q: A COPD patient receiving theophylline develops an irregular rhythm. ECG shows irregular RR intervals with 3 distinct P-wave morphologies. What is the most common cause and the first step in management?
opts: COPD / theophylline toxicity; Stop theophylline, then give beta-blocker/CCB to decrease heart rate
Digoxin toxicity; Administer digoxin-specific Fab fragments immediately
Severe hyperkalemia; Administer calcium gluconate followed by insulin-dextrose
Acute pulmonary embolism; Initiate systemic thrombolysis with alteplase
questions.exp: Multifocal AT: RR interval irregular + ≥ 3 P wave morphologies. m/c cause: COPD/theophylline. mx: Stop theophylline -> Beta-blocker/CCB: decrease HR. (Book p401)

questions.q: Under the types of atrial tachycardia listed on page 401, atrial tachycardia with AV block is classically associated with ____.
opts: digoxin
amiodarone
theophylline
verapamil
questions.exp: Under Types: Unifocal AT, Multifocal AT, and AT with AV block: A/w digoxin. (Book p401)

questions.q: An ECG rhythm strip shows atrial tachycardia with 2:1 AV block. How do the P waves and RR intervals appear on this tracing?
opts: Normal conducted P waves alternating with buried/missed P waves, producing an irregular RR interval
Uniformly absent P waves with a strictly regular ventricular rate > 200 bpm
Chaotic fibrillatory waves with no discernible discrete atrial deflections
Biphasic flutter waves at 300 bpm conducted in a constant 1:1 ratio
questions.exp: AT with AV block: Normal P wave + Buried P wave; Irregular RR. Tracing annotates conducted P (circles) and missed P (squares) in 2:1 AV block. (Book p402)

questions.q: In a narrow-complex tachycardia without visible P waves, what ventricular heart rate favors junctional tachycardia over AVNRT or AVRT?
opts: > 300 bpm
questions.exp: Junctional tachyarrhythmia: No P wave (seen in AVNRT, AVRT, Junctional tachycardia); HR ~ 100 - 110 bpm favors Junctional >> AVNRT/AVRT. (Book p402)

questions.q: According to the summary flowchart for narrow-complex tachycardia, which rhythm is classified under REGULAR R-R intervals rather than irregular R-R intervals?
opts: Sinus tachycardia
Multifocal atrial tachycardia
Atrial flutter with variable block
Atrial fibrillation
questions.exp: Irregular R-R: MAT, Atrial flutter with variable block, Atrial fibrillation, and Focal AT with varying block. Sinus tachycardia has regular R-R intervals. (Book p402)

questions.q: In regular narrow-complex tachycardias with present P waves, match each interval configuration to its diagnosis — 1) Short RP (< 80 ms), long PR 2) Short RP (> 80 ms), long PR 3) Long RP, short PR … A) AVNRT B) AVRT C) Atrial tachycardia
questions.exp: Summary tree: RP short, PR long -> AVRT (> 80 ms) and AVNRT; RP long, PR short -> Atrial tachycardia. (Book p402)
